title: Senior Companion Services
subtitle: Build a warm, reliable service without accidentally becoming a nurse, banker or emergency department

blocks.text: A good companion can make an afternoon brighter. A vague service agreement can make the same afternoon include three pharmacies, a ladder and somebody’s online banking password. We are choosing the first version.

Senior companion services are non-medical help: conversation, walks, errands, going along to appointments, light meal help and social outings. The business is built on trust, and trust needs clear limits. You must define what you include, check local business rules, plan for safety and turn down tasks that need health, personal care, legal or money authority.
Sell a defined visit, not “anything you need.” A written list of what you do protects the client, the family and you from mismatched expectations.

items.title: “Being kind is the only qualification needed.”
items.text: Kindness matters most, but reliability, limits, screening, clear communication, a safety plan and the right insurance keep kindness from being assigned a snow shovel at midnight.

blocks.text: Canada: Starting a business
A clear, written service lets you build a caring business that families trust and recommend.
blocks.detail: Deciding what you do, what you never do and what to charge protects your client and your income.
blocks.extra: Section 02 helps you write that line before your first visit.

sections.title: Write the Scope Before Setting the Rate

blocks.text: Draw the line between a kind gesture and a regulated task before the first visit, not during it.

items.title: USUALLY INCLUDED
items.text: Conversation, reading, games, walks, friendly check-ins, simple meal help, errands and going along to appointments, when your agreement allows them.

items.title: NEEDS A SEPARATE DECISION
items.text: Driving, using your own car, holding keys, pet care, lifting, bathing, medication reminders, cooking and entering an empty home. Each adds risk or needs training.

items.title: OUTSIDE A BASIC COMPANION SERVICE
items.text: Giving medication, wound care, transfers beyond what you can do safely, legal advice, banking, signing papers, holding passwords or acting under a power of attorney.

items.title: IN AN EMERGENCY
items.text: A companion watches and calls the agreed contact or 911. They do not diagnose, promise medical monitoring or make up a treatment plan.

blocks.text: A vulnerable sector check is different from a regular criminal record check. Your local police service sets the process, and a client or agency may need to confirm the job is a position of trust.

If you offer rides, check your licence class, your car’s condition, insurance for business use, how many passengers you can take and who pays for mileage. Personal car insurance may not cover business driving.
Ask an insurance broker about general liability insurance before your first client. If you will hold keys or enter empty homes, ask about bonding too. Many families and agencies will ask for proof.

items.title: “A companion can handle a client’s bank card if the family gives permission.”
items.text: Access to money creates serious risk of abuse and misunderstanding. Use receipts, small purchases approved ahead of time and ways to pay that never expose a PIN, password or broad authority.

blocks.text: RCMP: Criminal record checks

sections.title: Charge for the Whole Job, Not Only the Conversation

blocks.text: Your visit rate must cover planning, travel, parking, messages, record keeping, supplies, insurance, cancellations and unpaid gaps between clients. Start with a minimum visit length and a service area.

items.title: Set a minimum visit
items.text: Two hours is common. A 30-minute visit across town can cost you more in travel than it pays.

items.title: Add travel and parking
items.text: Charge a travel fee outside your service area, and track your kilometres for your taxes.

items.title: Write a cancellation rule
items.text: For example, 24 hours’ notice or a half-visit fee. A late cancellation is an unpaid gap in your day.

items.title: Count insurance and tax
items.text: Add your insurance cost to your rate, and set aside part of every payment for income tax and CPP.

blocks.text: Self-employment income must be reported even when clients pay by cash or e-transfer. Keep invoices, receipts, mileage records and a separate record of your business.
You generally do not have to charge GST/HST until your taxable sales pass $30,000 in one calendar quarter or over four quarters in a row. Check how your services are taxed before you hit that mark.
Tax basics for your first year

items.title: REPORT IT
items.text: Business income goes on Form T2125 with your personal tax return, whether clients pay by cash, cheque or e-transfer.

items.title: PAY BOTH HALVES OF CPP
items.text: Self-employed people pay the worker and employer shares of CPP, 11.9% of net business income above the basic amount, on Schedule 8 of the return.

items.title: SET MONEY ASIDE
items.text: Nobody takes tax off your pay. Move a share of every payment into a separate account. If you owe more than $3,000 ($1,800 in Quebec) this year and in either of the last two years, the CRA will ask for quarterly instalments.

items.title: KEEP RECORDS SIX YEARS
items.text: Keep invoices, receipts, mileage and bank records for six years from the end of the tax year they belong to.

items.title: “If the client pays cash, it is casual help rather than business income.”
items.text: How you are paid does not change what the income is. A toonie jar is charming. It is not an accounting exemption.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: a companion business succeeds by being specific. Define your non-medical tasks, check the home, price the full visit, protect money and personal information, and use a written plan for emergencies.
Meet Nadia
paragraphs: Nadia Singh starts a companion service in Mississauga. Her goal is three regular clients by spring, so she can leave her part-time retail job.

Her first client, Mr. Chen, wants weekly walks and grocery trips. On the first visit, his daughter hands Nadia his debit card and his PIN, “for convenience.” Convenience has arrived wearing a tiny financial-risk hat.
Then Nadia spots an unlabelled pill organizer beside the shopping list. The daughter asks her to “just make sure Dad takes the blue ones.”
Nadia feels the pull to say yes to both. She needs this client, and saying no on day one feels rude. Instead, she decides to offer a different plan before she leaves.

She suggests a store gift card the family loads with a set grocery amount. Nadia will bring back every receipt. For the pills, she explains that the pharmacy can blister-pack them, and the daughter can set reminders. Nadia will only note that a dose was missed and call the family.
The twist comes a month later. The daughter tells Nadia that a previous helper had used her dad’s card for her own shopping. The clear plan is why she trusts Nadia.
Mr. Chen gets his groceries and his conversation. Nadia keeps the client, gains two referrals from the family and never becomes an accidental bank branch with sensible shoes.

blocks.text: Use the payment method that gives you the least access and still works: the client pays at checkout, a store card, a set prepaid amount, or the family pays you back with receipts. Never keep a client’s PIN or online banking login.
What resolved the conflict?
Convenience is not a payment plan. Choose the payment method with the least access that still gets the groceries paid for.
Nadia kept her first client and gained two referrals by turning down the debit card and the pills.
blocks.detail: Offering a safer option, instead of a flat no, protects your clients and your reputation.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next move.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why should a companion service write down what it does not do?
items.detail: A written list of included and excluded tasks protects the client, the family and you from mismatched expectations.

items.title: When might a vulnerable sector check be needed?
items.detail: When the job is a position of trust with vulnerable people. Your local police service sets the process, which is different from a regular record check.

items.title: Why should banking and passwords stay out of your service?
items.detail: Access to money creates serious risk of abuse and misunderstanding. Safer options are receipts, approved purchases and ways to pay that never expose a PIN or password.

items.title: Which costs belong in your visit price besides time with the client?
items.detail: Planning, travel, parking, messages, record keeping, supplies, insurance, cancellations, unpaid gaps between clients, and money set aside for tax and CPP.

items.title: What should a companion do in a medical emergency?
items.detail: Watch and call the agreed contact or 911. Do not diagnose, promise medical monitoring or make up a treatment plan.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Safe Service Launch Plan

blocks.text: Describe services only. Do not write client health numbers, bank details, passwords, door codes or medical histories here.
Working alone in a private home needs a check-in plan. Share your visit times with a trusted contact and agree what happens if you do not check in, without sharing the client’s private details.

items.title: Companion service
items.text: Non-medical social and practical help.

items.title: Scope of service
items.text: The written list of tasks you include and exclude.

items.title: Vulnerable sector check
items.text: A special police record check for positions of trust.

items.title: Incident record
items.text: A short, factual note about something unexpected or unsafe.

items.title: Working alone plan
items.text: A check-in and response plan for someone working with no help nearby.

items.title: Minimum visit
items.text: The shortest appointment you charge for.

items.title: Self-employment income
items.text: Business income you earn working for yourself.

quiz.question: True or False: “Being kind is the only qualification needed.”

questions: Who is your ideal client, and what will a visit include? A sentence or two is fine.
Which tasks will you always say no to or refer elsewhere? For example, giving medication or banking.
What will you charge, how long is your minimum visit, and what is your cancellation rule?
Do you have insurance, and have you started a vulnerable sector check? (Both / One / Neither yet / Not sure)
How will groceries and errands be paid for without you holding a card or PIN?
Who is your check-in contact for visits, and where will you find your first three clients?
samples: Seniors living alone in my area. Walks, chats, errands and appointments.
Giving medication, bathing, banking and signing papers.
$34 an hour, two-hour minimum, 24 hours’ notice to cancel.
Neither yet. I am calling a broker and my police service this week.
A store card the family loads, and I return every receipt.
My sister. A seniors’ centre, my church and a local pharmacy board.
